extracted.intended_audience: shippers, carriers, manufacturers, and regulators of radioactive/Class 7 hazardous materials; industry stakeholders and commenters on DOT/HMR rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble/explanatory guidance for amendments to the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR) governing transport of Class 7 (radioactive) materials, explaining new exemption values, A1/A2 packaging limits, NORM/ore exceptions, and hazard-communication and marking requirements. Intended to guide regulated parties and inform notice-and-comment participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of radionuclide-specific exemption values (TS-R-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting the TS-R-1 exemption values to replace the 70 Bq/g criterion for determining when radioactive material will be regulated as a Class 7 hazardous material (with specified exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: hazards are related to dose, not simply activity concentration; modeling for 20 representative radionuclides shows average modeled annual worker dose would decrease from ~0.5 mSv to ~0.23 mSv under the proposed exemption activity concentrations (about a 50% reduction). Agency balanced safety and economic burden concerns. Note exception described for ores and natural materials (10× rule) and retained some domestic exceptions (e.g., Mo-99, Cf-252). Commenters' concerns (e.g., higher numeric exemption for some nuclides versus 70 Bq/g) are addressed by dose-based risk considerations and harmonization benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative shipment of borderline batches (treat as LSA‑I)
rubrics_metrics.description: In borderline cases where some batches exceed exemption values and others do not, it may be simpler to determine whether any of the material exceeds the LSA‑I limits and, if not, treat the material conservatively and ship it as LSA‑I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicality rationale: shipping as LSA‑I simplifies compliance even though the material becomes regulated under HMR; existing regulations for domestic shipments of LSA‑I have relatively modest communication and packaging requirements. This approach avoids costly isotopic analyses in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10× exemption for natural materials and ores
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural materials or ores that contain naturally occurring radionuclides will be regulated as Class 7 only if both their activity concentrations and consignment activities are greater than 10 times the corresponding exemption values in §173.436.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: 10× chosen to balance radiological protection and practical inconvenience of regulating large quantities of low-activity materials. Examples included: cement, coal, fertilizers, non-radioactive metals, gypsum, residues from mining and smelting. Agency expects material with low radiological hazard not to be unnecessarily regulated; commenters urged inclusion of tailings, secondary materials, and wastes in this exemption. If states/permits use the 70 Bq/g limit to prevent radioactive waste acceptance, they may need to change their requirements if DOT adopts TS-R-1 values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of intended use for exemptions between 1× and 10×
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the exemption between 1 and 10 times the activity concentration values is allowed for ores containing small amounts of activity when these ores are not intended to be used for their radioactive properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency recognizes the 'intended use' test can be difficult to apply and prefers to minimize burden on shippers/carriers. While one commenter argued intended use should not factor into transport regulation, the final rule allows the exemption where ores are not mined for radioactivity. Agency accepts that intended use does not change the low transport risk, but acknowledges enforcement/application challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for determining 'estimated average activity' for 10× exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested criterion to determine the estimated average activity for applying the 10× exemption: divide material into 10 or more equal volumes (each ≤ 0.1 m3) and average specific activities when differences between all pairs do not vary by more than a factor of 10; if larger differences exist, average the highest volume with the next nine highest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure follows NUREG-1608/RSPA Advisory Guidance 97-005 (section 4.2.3) for 'distributed throughout' material. If the average so computed is no greater than 10× the exemption activity concentration in §173.436, the material qualifies for the 10× exemption. Advice: avoid using a simple overall average that masks localized higher-activity volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt revised A1 and A2 values (Q system / TS‑R‑1) with specified domestic exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt new A1 and A2 values based on the updated Q system (IAEA TS‑R‑1 / ICRP Publication 60 dosimetric models and updated biokinetic data), with domestic exceptions retaining A2 = 0.74 TBq (20 Ci) for Mo‑99 and A1 = 0.1 TBq (2.7 Ci) and A2 = 0.001 TBq (0.027 Ci) for Cf‑252.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background: the Q system incorporates external photon, external beta, inhalation, skin/ingestion contamination, and submersion in gaseous radionuclide pathways; updates yield different A1/A2 values reflecting revised dose assessments. Agency will adopt TS‑R‑1 values generally but retain limited U.S. domestic exceptions to avoid undue economic or safety consequences. For international shipments, TS‑R‑1 A1/A2 values apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for determining A1/A2 for nuclides not in TS‑R‑1
rubrics_metrics.description: Radionuclides absent from TS‑R‑1 tables are removed from §173.435; shippers must determine A1/A2 per §173.433, which may require Associate Administrator approval or use of prescribed tables/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: some nuclides excluded from TS‑R‑1 due to uncertainties in decay schemes or biokinetic models. Request for A1/A2 for unlisted nuclides should be addressed to the Associate Administrator with appropriate justification; determinations are expected to follow the Q system guidelines in Appendix I to TS‑G‑1.1. The rule text was clarified to reflect approval requirements when using A2 values related to solubility class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of decay-chain daughters for activity reporting and packaging selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When A1 or A2 values include contributions from daughter nuclides with half lives less than 10 days and no daughter has a half life greater than that of the parent, the parent and those daughters are to be treated as a single radionuclide for packaging selection and for the 'total activity' required on shipping papers and Radioactive Yellow II/III labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency reasoning: A1/A2 values assigned to parents have been adjusted to represent the hazard of the chain. Practical implications: the 'total' activity listed may sometimes be less than the true activity contents, but the decay-chain hazard is correctly accounted for in packaging selection. Short‑half‑life daughters so treated need not be listed individually nor included in the §173.433(f) 95% formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard communication: harmonize proper shipping names and UN numbers to TS‑R‑1
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow only the use of proper shipping names and UN identification numbers established in TS‑R‑1 and international modal regulations in the Hazardous Materials Table; remove 'D' symbols and the 'I' for remaining Class 7 entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency will not adopt domestic use of Type C package names/UN numbers or those for fissile LSA/SCO materials. This harmonization supports import/export consistency and reuse of previously imported packagings. Some prior domestic distinctions (D/I symbols) are eliminated to simplify alignment with international standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking requirements for excepted, industrial, and Type A packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Require marking of UN identification numbers on excepted packages; require marking of package type and international vehicle registration code (e.g., 'USA') on all industrial and Type A packages; require marking of packaging manufacturer on Type A packages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: improve traceability and harmonize domestic practice with TS‑R‑1. Commenters argued marking excepted/empty packages with UN numbers would not materially aid emergency responders; agency concluded the harmonization benefit justifies the requirement despite small marginal safety benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity unit formatting on shipping papers and labels
rubrics_metrics.description: If customary activity units (curies, or fractions thereof) are used in shipping paper descriptions or on radioactive labels, they must be enclosed in parentheses following the required SI units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standardizes unit presentation and emphasizes SI units as primary. Ensures consistency across shipping documents and labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce Criticality Safety Index (CSI) and fissile labeling; restrict TI to radiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a Criticality Safety Index (CSI) to express the former criticality control transport index and require a fissile label displaying the CSI; restrict the term Transport Index (TI) to the former radiation TI (derived solely from the max radiation dose rate at 1 m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: uncoupling of radiation and criticality hazards simplifies package grouping and transport decisions; fissile label makes fissile contents obvious and aids handling. The CSI will replace the former criticality TI while TI will denote only radiation-based index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark industrial packagings with TYPE IP-1, TYPE IP-2, or TYPE IP-3
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a requirement to mark industrial packagings with the markings TYPE IP-1, TYPE IP-2 or TYPE IP-3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This marking standardizes identification of industrial packaging performance classes to support consistent handling and regulatory oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require 'Radioactive-LSA'/'Radioactive-SCO' and 'RQ' markings on all Class 7 packages containing LSA or SCO
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Radioactive-LSA' or 'Radioactive-SCO' and 'RQ' markings, when appropriate, must be placed on all Class 7 material packages containing LSA material or SCO, independent of their weight or capacity (i.e., both bulk and non-bulk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency clarified intention in response to commenter confusion: marking is required on both bulk and non-bulk packages. This ensures consistent communication of regulated LSA/SCO shipments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excepted instrument/article marking: international vs domestic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Excepted packages of instruments and articles containing small quantities of radioactive material must have the 'RADIOACTIVE' marking when transported under IAEA Regulations (TS‑R‑1), ICAO Technical Instructions, or IMDG Code; however, agency declined to require marking the product itself 'RADIOACTIVE' for NRC-exempt distribution products domestically where such marking would be burdensome or impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued small consumer items (e.g., HID lamps, glow switches) are NRC-exempt distribution licensed and marking the product would be impractical and counterproductive. Agency agrees product marking is not adopted domestically for such items but notes excepted packages used for international transport still require 'RADIOACTIVE' marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of overpack label category (TI + highest inner package surface dose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Label category for a rigid overpack is to be determined by the Transport Index (TI) as determined by adding individual indices or direct measurement, and the highest surface radiation level on an individual package inside the overpack, unless the overpack has been demonstrated to satisfy the packaging requirements for the package type appropriate for the totality of its contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical impact: using the highest interior package surface dose in label determination could result in an overpack requiring a Yellow‑III label even if the overpack's measured TI corresponds to Yellow‑II or White‑I, potentially triggering placarding and CDL/registered-shipper burdens. Commenters argued this could discourage use of overpacks and increase worker exposures; agency retained the formulation but noted the option to demonstrate overpack meets packaging requirements to avoid this outcome.
